quotes.text: Attribute quality is the first architecture decision, not the last one. Most teams treat it as cleanup.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Puts identity data quality at the start of governance design.

quotes.text: The old model says access is permanent unless someone remembers to kill it. This model says access is temporary unless someone renews it.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Summarizes the shift to expiry-by-default access.

quotes.text: That's where it breaks. The system measures completion, not judgment. Completion is easy to count. It's a yes or a no. Judgment is hard to see.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Explains why rubber-stamped access reviews pass audits but change nothing.

quotes.text: scheduled governance asks has anything gone wrong since we last checked? Event driven governance acts when something changes, you need both.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Clear contrast between calendar-driven reviews and event-driven lifecycle workflows.

quotes.text: An admin account with permanent rights is permanent attack surface every hour of every day.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Makes the case against standing admin access in one sentence.

takeaways: Entra ID Governance works when it is designed around real behavior: named owners, safe defaults and review tasks small enough to finish.
Access packages with expiry, scoped access reviews with recommendations and auto-apply, and lifecycle workflows driven by clean HR attributes replace the yearly cleanup.
Privileged roles should be eligible and activated just in time through PIM, and the whole program should be rolled out in phases starting with data quality.
hook: Access that is never reviewed keeps growing, and yearly recertifications end in rubber stamps. This episode shows identity architects, IAM and compliance teams how access packages, access reviews, lifecycle workflows and PIM in Microsoft Entra ID Governance work together as one event-driven system.
